role: Chairman, Department of Physical Sciences; Associate Director, Joint Center for Environmental and Urban Problems, Florida International University
stance_basis: opens letter stating environmental preservation requires elimination of ORV as recreational vehicles
summary: Ruth F. Weiner, writing on behalf of Florida International University, argues that ORV use on public lands is inherently damaging and should ideally be eliminated as a recreational activity. While acknowledging BOR's apparent compulsion to permit some ORV use, she calls for significantly more stringent criteria including blanket restrictions above timberline, mandatory federal registration, a minimum operator age of 16, fees for all ORV use, prohibition in wildlife refuges during vulnerable seasons, and stricter limits on exhaust pollutants. She expresses strong personal opposition to ORV users and urges federal agencies to limit and discourage recreational ORV use.
complaint_summary: Weiner argues that ORV use inherently damages terrain and should be eliminated as a recreational activity, and calls for numerous more stringent restrictions including blanket prohibitions above timberline, mandatory federal registration, a minimum operator age of 16, fees for all ORV use, prohibition in wildlife refuges during vulnerable seasons, and stricter limits on exhaust pollutants.

statement.text:
I would like to make the following comments on the draft environmental impact statement for the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644:
First of all, it must be recognized that off-the-road vehicles (ORV), when used off of roads, cause damage to the terrain over which they travel. Environmental preservation really ought to require elimination of ORV as recreational vehicles (I am here excluding use of ORV in game patrolling, ski-patrol, or other non-recreational uses). There is no way to use an ORV that will not "adversely affect---natural, aesthetic, or scenic values" or wildlife in the area. The claim that ORV have positive values in the form of "strengthening family ties" (as stated on p. 12 of the impact statement) is spurious to the argument: families hike together, cross-country ski together, ride horses together, snowshoe together, and do any number of outdoor things which do not require, and are in fact disrupted by, ORV. BOR obviously feels some compulsion to permit ORV use, however. With this in mind, the criteria for their use should be made more stringent in several ways.
Distinctions must be made among various ORV. Jeeps and other four-wheel drive regular-pressure tire vehicles ought not to be considered ORV for recreational purposes: the damage they cause is much too extensive to sanction use except on roads and "jeep trails." Some additional blanket restrictions should also be made. No recreational use of ORV should be permitted above timberline, with the elevation of "timberline" determined by USGS or some other knowledgeable agency. (Even snowmobiles cause damage by packing snow in tundra regions, where the snow melts late in summer anyway.) Damage to tundra by trailbikes, etc., is generally permanent.

All ORV used on Federal lands should be registered, and have the registration number clearly displayed on the vehicle. State laws are frequently inadequate, and in many cases there is no state law requiring registration. If the vehicle is not registered how is one to apprehend violators? Similarly, state regulations on operators are not strict enough, as a rule. In Colorado a 10-year-old can legally operate a snowmobile. Such a child has not, in my opinion, sufficiently mature judgment to operate a vehicle capable of speeds up to 60 m.p.h., even if he may have the requisite mechanical skills. The Federal government should put a lower age limit of 16 years on operation of ORV on Federal lands. The motor vehicle license provision set out in the impact statement is good, and there should be no exception to it.
ORV rallies or other events should be limited to ungraded roads or areas where there is already considerable evidence of vehicular use. Such events are considerably more damaging to the environment than trail use. Fees for <u>all</u> ORV use should be established, in addition to fees for rallies or other events. Trail-bikes do infinitely more damage to trails than hikers, and considerably more than horses, and there is no reason they should not be charged for its repair.
The effect of ORV on wildlife is especially damaging; the effect of snowmobiles on wintering <u>cervidae</u> is disastrous. The Colorado Department of Game, Fish and Parks testified repeatedly to deer and elk deaths directly attributable to frightening or harassment by snowmobiles. Similarly, indiscriminate use of airboats in the Everglades during the dry season can drive amphibians far from watering places. Use of ORV in wildlife refuges should be prohibited, at least during those seasons when the animals in the refuge are weakest.
The impact of air and water pollutants produced by ORV is minimized in the draft impact statement. These are not "likely to increase with the number of vehicles involved" (p. 14), they are certain to increase with the number of vehicles involved, and in direct proportion to that number! When the impact of these of these pollutants becomes noticeable, it will be too late to do anything about their presence. We must take preventive action and severely limit the concentration of exhaust pollutants permitted. We must also remember that, in general, the flora and fauna exposed to ORV are exceedingly fragile.
My personal experience with ORV users is that they are almost uniformly rude, careless, and of dirty habits, especially when compared as a group with hikers. You can generally trace a snowmobile track or motorbike trail by the litter. They are disdainful of and discourteous to those who prefer non-mechanized forms of travel. My children have several times come close to severe injury from being run down by a snowmobile while cross-country skiing. Why should it be necessary for anyone to "experience an exhilarating feeling of freedom ...at high speeds..." if doing so means wrecking the surrounding environment and endangering the lives and safety of animals and walking humans? I would Sike to see some evidence that "family relationships are strengthened" (p.18) by this activity and then determine whether it is worth the price! I am happy to see BOR admit unequivocally that "land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use." Recreational ORV use may be with us to stay, but I hope that the Federal agencies involved will do what they can to limit and discourage it, since they seem to be quite aware of its detrimental impact.

I hope these comments will be of assistance to you.
Sincerely,
Ruth F. Weiner
